items.title: The Missing Link Between Open Source and the Wallet on Your Phone
items.summary: What connects public source code to the app you install? A practical guide to reproducible builds, signed releases, App Store approval, and Oath’s current evidence.
items.content_html:
You find a wallet with a public GitHub repository. The code is there. The license is there. People can inspect it, discuss it, and build it themselves. That is a meaningful reason to pay attention.

Then you open the App Store and tap Download.

One question still needs an answer: was the app you just installed actually built from the code you were shown?

For a wallet, that question reaches all the way to your money. The software on your phone helps generate or import credentials, displays the transaction you are about to authorize, and signs it. Being able to inspect the source is valuable. Being able to connect that source to the distributed app adds another layer of assurance.

Here is what that extra layer means, what it can prove, and how Oath describes the relationship between its public source and its App Store release.

What open source gives you

Open-source software makes its code available under a license that grants rights to use, study, modify, and redistribute it. The Open Source Initiative’s definition includes those freedoms; simply putting some code on a public page does not automatically meet the definition. Read the Open Source Definition.

For a wallet, public source lets independent developers examine questions that a marketing page cannot settle. How are keys generated? What gets stored? What leaves the device? What must happen before a transaction is signed? Which third-party libraries are involved?

That scrutiny matters even if you never read a line of code yourself. Researchers and other developers can investigate on your behalf and publish findings that everyone can inspect.

But a repository describes a body of code. On its own, it does not establish which code produced a particular download. A developer could publish one version and distribute another. A build system could also introduce an unwanted change after a reviewer has examined the source. Those are the gaps that build verification aims to reduce. The Reproducible Builds project explains this threat.

What a reproducible build adds

A build turns source code into the software your device runs. A reproducible build makes that transformation repeatable: with the specified source, environment, and instructions, another party can produce identical copies of the defined output files. The comparison is usually made using cryptographic hashes. See the formal definition.

A meaningful verification result therefore connects three things: an exact source revision, a documented build process, and a precisely identified release artifact. The report should show what was compared and whether it matched.

There is an extra step when the claim concerns an app store. Matching an unsigned file hosted on GitHub establishes a result about that file. To establish a result about the app on your phone, the evidence must also connect the comparison to the artifact delivered through that store.

Consider two otherwise comparable wallets. Both publish their source. For one, the connection between source and download rests on the publisher’s assurance. For the other, an independent party can rebuild the stated release and verify the distributed artifact using a documented method. The second offers stronger evidence against an undisclosed difference introduced during building or distribution. That is the specific security advantage.

The word “verified” needs an object

Several useful checks are often described with the same word. They answer different questions.

A verified GitHub commit means GitHub has verified a commit’s cryptographic signature. It says something about the origin and integrity of that commit. It does not compare an App Store download with the repository. GitHub documents exactly what its badge means.

A successful build or test run establishes that the stated build or tests completed in that environment. It does not establish that a store serves the same output.

A signed release provides evidence about the signer and the integrity of the signed artifact. A developer’s signature does not, by itself, demonstrate that the artifact was produced from public source.

A build attestation records provenance: information such as the source commit, repository, and workflow associated with an artifact. This is valuable evidence, but it still needs verification against the artifact and a sensible trust policy. GitHub explicitly warns that attestations do not guarantee an artifact is secure. Read GitHub’s explanation of artifact attestations.

An independently reproduced release adds a rebuild-and-compare result. A claim about the store version must identify how that result reaches the store-delivered app.

Before accepting “verified build,” ask: verified by whom, against what, and for which version?

Apple’s approval and the source-to-store question

Apple’s review and code-signing system provide real protections. Apple describes developer identity checks, mandatory code signing, and review intended to check that apps generally work as described. These establish a controlled distribution process. They do not constitute a published comparison with a wallet’s GitHub source. Apple explains its app code-signing process.

The artifact itself also needs careful treatment. Apple’s app-thinning documentation describes device-specific variants containing different combinations of assets and binaries. A universal archive and a device-specific download can therefore be different files for legitimate reasons. See Apple’s documentation on app variants.

A credible iOS verification method must identify the exact version and build, the source revision, the toolchain and configuration, and the particular artifact or components compared. It must explain how platform packaging and signing are handled. If any parts are excluded from comparison, the report needs to say which parts and why.

A matching version number, an archive checksum, or a successful upload is useful release bookkeeping. None of those facts alone closes the source-to-store gap.

When a wallet says its App Store build is verified, you should be able to follow a method and inspect a result, rather than infer a result from Apple’s approval.

Google Play needs a precise claim, too

Android has practical tools for reproducible verification, but the distribution route still matters. Google Play can generate and sign optimized APKs from an Android App Bundle for different device configurations. Verifying an APK from a project’s website does not automatically verify every Play-delivered variant. Google explains how App Bundles are distributed.

F-Droid documents a concrete approach: reproduce the upstream APK, copy its signing information using the supported method, and check that verification succeeds. Its documentation explains both the required equivalence and common causes of mismatches. That is the kind of inspectable process a reproducibility claim should point to. Read F-Droid’s reproducible-build documentation.

How to compare wallets fairly

There are useful examples worth recognizing. Muun’s Android repository includes instructions for reproducible builds and for checking an existing APK: obtain the installed APK, select the corresponding source commit, and run its verification script. That goes beyond a general statement that the source is public. This article reviews the published procedure; it does not report a fresh verification of Muun’s current release, and the Android procedure should not be treated as proof for iOS. Muun’s Android build and verification instructions.

Blockstream’s Android README documents another useful check: verifying release authenticity through certificate fingerprints and signed checksums. Those instructions help authenticate the download. The check described there answers a different question from independently rebuilding it. This is a distinction between the methods, not a claim that those instructions describe all of Blockstream’s security work. Blockstream’s release-authenticity instructions.

For any wallet that offers only a repository link, the fair conclusion is limited: public source is available, but that link alone supplies no evidence of a store-binary match. It would be wrong to turn that absence into an accusation of malicious behavior. It would also be wrong to advertise a match without evidence.

Compare the platform, release, method, and result. A brand-wide label hides too much.

Oath: open source, and a clear statement about the shipped app

Oath publishes its MIT-licensed 4.1.14 (98) source release with build instructions and a release verification record. The app source used for the uploaded archive is commit v4.1.14. Provider configuration and Apple signing are supplied locally and excluded from Git. Explore Oath’s published source release.

On October 30, 2026, build 86 was uploaded to App Store Connect and submitted for review. The release verification record records the source, archive and upload evidence. Apple showed Waiting for Review at submission; the public US App Store listing still showed 4.1.2 when checked. Submission is not approval or a new public-store binary comparison.

There is a distinction worth keeping explicit: a publisher’s confirmation is not the same evidence as an independent party reproducing a release and publishing its comparison. This article does not present a new binary comparison, a byte-for-byte reproducibility result, or an independent security audit. The repository’s documented exclusions and configuration requirements still apply.

That distinction is the point of this article. Public source gives people something concrete to inspect. A maintainer’s release statement makes the team’s claim explicit. An independently repeatable comparison provides a further level of evidence. Readers should be able to tell which of those they are looking at.

For Oath, as for every wallet, security language should help people understand the evidence. It should never make them guess what “verified” means.

Five things to look for before trusting a build claim

  1. An exact release. The platform, version, build number, and distribution channel should be unambiguous.
  2. An exact source revision. A fixed commit is more useful than a moving default branch.
  3. A repeatable recipe. Toolchain versions, dependencies, configuration, and required build inputs should be documented.
  4. A transparent comparison. Look for artifact identifiers, the comparison method, the result, and any exclusions.
  5. A named verifier and a date. Distinguish a publisher’s own checks from independent reproduction, and check whether the result applies to the version you use.

The Reproducible Builds guidance on build environments explains why the toolchain and its assumptions need to be documented.

You should never need to share a recovery phrase or private key to investigate a public build-verification claim.

Better evidence, with honest limits

A reproducible build can faithfully reproduce vulnerable code. It cannot, by itself, establish that the design is sound, that a remote service is trustworthy, or that your phone is uncompromised. Source review, security testing, careful dependency management, and responsible release practices still matter. Reproducibility addresses a particular gap in that larger system. Read more about its purpose and limits.

Open source makes inspection possible. Reproducible builds make a specified source-to-artifact relationship testable. Verification of the distributed app brings that evidence closer to the software you actually use.

For self-custody, those distinctions deserve plain language. A wallet should make it easy to see what has been checked, what the result proves, and what remains unproven. Confidence is more useful when you can trace where it comes from.

Published October 19, 2026. Oath release evidence updated October 30, 2026. Oath’s source-correspondence statement is supplied by its maintainers. The technical explanations cite public documentation; this article is not an independent wallet audit or a new reproduction of an App Store or Google Play release.

items.title: Your Crypto, Their Permission: The $388 Million Bitget Wake-Up Call
items.summary: Bitget’s $388 million breach exposes the difference between a protected balance and control of your money. A sourced examination of exchange failures, self-custody, and the responsibilities that come with your keys.
items.content_html:
An exchange can promise to replace stolen money. It cannot give you back the moment you needed to move it.

That distinction is easy to overlook when markets are calm. Your balance appears on a screen. You can buy, sell, and watch its value change. The experience feels like possession. Only when withdrawals stop does the underlying arrangement become visible: someone else has the authority to release your assets.

Bitget’s September 24 security breach has made that arrangement painfully concrete. The exchange initially estimated the loss at $351.6 million, then revised it to $387.5 million after identifying additional affected transfers. Its latest public account rounds the figure to approximately $388 million. These are estimates of assets taken from exchange infrastructure—not evidence that customers individually suffered equivalent, unreimbursed losses. Bitget’s September 25 update; updated incident account.

The distinction matters. So does the fact that customers could not withdraw while the exchange repaired its systems.

We build Oath Wallet because we believe people should be able to hold and use their crypto without relying on an exchange’s permission. But the case for self-custody deserves more than a slogan, and readers deserve more than a frightening headline. It requires a careful account of what failed, what an exchange can actually promise, and which responsibilities move to you when you take control of your keys.

What actually happened at Bitget

The incident affected Bitget’s centralized exchange. Bitget Wallet, its separate non-custodial product, was not affected, according to Bitget. Confusing those products would obscure the very distinction this story illustrates. Bitget’s incident account.

The exchange’s September 25 update reported unauthorized transfers across several networks, including assets on Ethereum and other EVM chains, XRP Ledger, Zcash, and TRON. The upward revision from $351.6 million to $387.5 million reflected a fuller accounting, including Zcash and TRON transfers omitted initially. Bitget said the revision did not indicate a second attack or further transfers after containment. It also announced recovery bounties for qualifying assistance in freezing or recovering funds. Official fund-tracing and recovery update.

The attackers did not necessarily need to steal the keys

Bitget’s current explanation is preliminary: an attacker may have exploited a third-party security product to obtain privileged internal credentials, then used them to issue fraudulent withdrawal commands. The exchange says private-key compromise has been ruled out in its investigation to date, and its cold wallets were unaffected. Mandiant and SlowMist are supporting the continuing investigation. Bitget’s incident account.

Blockchain investigator TRM Labs described the reported failure as manipulation of the information used to authorize transfers. Its analysis also traced the dispersal of stolen funds and routes through cross-chain services. TRM identified links suggesting North Korean involvement but stopped short of definitive attribution. That uncertainty belongs in any responsible account of the breach. TRM Labs’ analysis.

The security lesson is broader than the identity of the attacker. A private key can remain secret while the machinery surrounding it authorizes a disastrous transaction. A signing system answers a cryptographic question: was this transaction approved by the required key? It does not, by itself, establish that the human intention behind the transaction was honest or correctly understood.

For an exchange customer, this creates a difficult boundary. You can secure your password, protect your email, and use strong authentication. You cannot personally inspect every privileged credential, third-party dependency, withdrawal rule, or internal approval process at the exchange. Your account security and the institution’s custody security are related, but they are different systems.

The pause exposed who controlled access

Bitget’s updated chronology places the first unauthorized transfers at 18:31 UTC on September 24. It says reconciliation detected a discrepancy and automatically blocked withdrawals at 19:05; withdrawal and signing services were shut down at 21:44. These are the company’s reported timings, not our independent forensic reconstruction. Updated incident timeline.

Pausing a compromised withdrawal system can be the responsible response. Continuing to operate it could expose more assets. The problem for customers is that the same measure needed to protect the collective pool also prevents an individual from leaving it.

That is a structural limitation of custodial protection. A platform can have a good reason to suspend withdrawals, yet the customer still loses the ability to act. There need be no dishonesty, insolvency, or malicious intent for this loss of control to occur.

The recovery is part of the story, too

Bitget says customer balances remain unaffected and its Protection Fund covers the incident’s financial impact. Its published schedule proposed reopening BTC withdrawals on September 28, ETH on September 29, USDT on September 30, and remaining supported tokens, fiat withdrawals, and P2P services on October 2, each at 08:00 UTC. Those later dates remain a schedule, not completed milestones as of this article. Bitget’s withdrawal announcement.

On September 28, The Block reported that Bitget had begun processing Bitcoin withdrawals as scheduled. That is meaningful progress and should be acknowledged plainly. This is an account of a breach and a staged restoration of access—not a claim that Bitget has collapsed or that all customer money is gone. The Block’s September 28 report.

Nevertheless, restoring access after an interruption is different from having maintained it. Consider a person who needs to pay a supplier, meet an obligation, or move funds into a safer arrangement. Even if their eventual balance is preserved, their choices during the interruption were constrained. This is an illustration of the risk, not a claim about a particular Bitget customer.

A complete definition of protection must include access as well as reimbursement.

A protection fund is useful. It does not confer control.

A sufficiently funded reserve can prevent a platform theft from becoming a customer loss. Customers should welcome that protection. TRM’s September 25 account cited a Bitget protection fund of approximately $464 million and the exchange’s statement that it covered the loss. That is a reported figure from that date, not a claim about the fund’s balance today. TRM Labs.

But a reserve changes who may absorb a financial loss; it does not change who authorizes withdrawals. The customer still depends on the institution to assess the incident, deploy resources, repair infrastructure, and restore service.

When evaluating any protection fund, useful questions concern its assets, custody, scope, exclusions, legal commitments, and ability to cover multiple events. A headline dollar amount cannot answer those questions on its own. Nor should a privately maintained fund be casually described as equivalent to government deposit insurance.

The same discipline applies to proof of reserves. The PCAOB’s Office of the Investor Advocate has warned that these reports are not audits and may omit liabilities, asset-holder rights, borrowed reserves, and the effectiveness of governance or internal controls. They are also tied to a point in time. PCAOB investor advisory.

An exchange can hold substantial assets and still suffer a failure in the process that moves them. Financial resilience and operational security answer different questions. Neither gives a depositor a personal signing key for the exchange’s pooled funds.

Three earlier failures, three different warnings

It would be misleading to treat every exchange crisis as the same event. Theft, fraud, and prolonged insolvency proceedings have different causes and different outcomes. They nevertheless expose a recurring dependency: customers must wait for decisions made elsewhere.

Mt. Gox: the cost measured in years

Mt. Gox’s trustee was already reporting on bankruptcy proceedings and the recovery of assets in July 2014. A decade later, in June 2024, the rehabilitation trustee announced that Bitcoin and Bitcoin Cash repayments would begin that July. The notice described the technical, regulatory, and coordination work required before repayment. 2014 trustee report; 2024 repayment notice.

The lesson is not captured by a missing-coin total alone. It is the interval between believing an asset is available and having the freedom to use what can eventually be recovered.

During such an interval, an owner’s life continues. Expenses arrive; circumstances change. A claim handled through a rehabilitation process is not operationally equivalent to bitcoin that the holder can transfer. Eventual distributions matter, but they do not erase the years in between.

FTX: account security could not stop insider misuse

FTX illustrates a different failure. In March 2024, the U.S. Department of Justice announced Sam Bankman-Fried’s 25-year prison sentence. It described the misappropriation of billions of dollars deposited by customers, including their use for investments, political contributions, and repayment of Alameda Research’s debts. Prosecutors put the theft of customer money at more than $8 billion. U.S. Department of Justice.

No customer could fix that arrangement by choosing a stronger login password. The central problem was what people inside the institution could do with assets entrusted to them.

This does not establish that other exchanges behave like FTX. It establishes why custody requires scrutiny of governance, segregation, legal rights, and business incentives—not merely the appearance of a polished application. A clean interface tells you little about authority behind it.

Bybit: cold storage still depended on a signing workflow

The FBI attributed the theft of approximately $1.5 billion from Bybit on or about February 21, 2025, to North Korea. Bybit subsequently reported that compromised credentials belonging to a Safe developer enabled an attack that deceived signers into approving a malicious transaction. FBI public notice; Bybit’s February 26 investigation update.

Cold storage reduces exposure, but assets eventually have to move. The process that interprets and authorizes that movement remains part of the security system. This is relevant to institutions and individual users alike: multiple signatures and protected keys are valuable, but they cannot make an inaccurately understood transaction safe.

Mt. Gox, FTX, Bybit, and Bitget should not be collapsed into one accusation. Their shared lesson is narrower and stronger: control of assets depends on the entire custody arrangement, including the people, software, and procedures permitted to move them.

What self-custody changes

A wallet does not literally contain coins. It manages the keys and related information needed to interact with assets recorded on a blockchain. With genuine self-custody, you control the credentials that authorize spending instead of asking an exchange to authorize a withdrawal. The SEC’s custody bulletin explains this distinction and the responsibilities it creates. Investor.gov: crypto asset custody basics.

That change has several practical consequences.

An exchange’s withdrawal policy stops governing those assets. Once assets have been transferred to a wallet you control, a trading platform cannot impose its own withdrawal queue on that wallet. Your ability to transact still depends on the network, fees, valid credentials, and the rules of the asset itself.

The exchange’s balance sheet stops being the custody foundation for those holdings. If you keep native assets under your own keys, you do not need that exchange to remain solvent to authorize a transaction. This advantage disappears for funds you subsequently deposit into a custodial service. It also should not be confused with eliminating the separate risks of stablecoin issuers, bridges, or lending protocols.

You can choose how much authority to expose. Daily spending, long-term holdings, and experimental applications do not have to share one wallet. Separating them can limit the consequences of a mistake. Merely adding more accounts derived from the same exposed recovery phrase does not provide that isolation.

Recovery can be designed around credentials you control. For a standard recovery-phrase wallet, retaining the correct phrase—and any additional passphrase and necessary account information—can allow restoration in compatible software. Compatibility and the precise backup requirements must be checked before they are needed.

These are concrete reasons self-custody can be a better arrangement for long-term holders who are prepared to manage it. It removes the exchange’s discretionary control over the assets held that way. It does not make every transaction, token, device, or wallet safe.

The responsibilities that come with the keys

A serious defense of self-custody must address its failures as carefully as those of exchanges.

If your recovery material is stolen, an attacker may gain the same spending authority you have. If the only usable recovery material is lost, there may be no institution able to restore access. The SEC’s custody guidance emphasizes that self-custody places responsibility for private-key security on the holder. Investor.gov custody bulletin.

And a key need not be stolen for a user to approve something harmful. In December 2023, the Ledger Connect Kit incident injected malicious code into applications using the affected library and tricked users into signing asset-draining transactions, according to Ledger’s incident report. That was an attack on a connection and signing experience, not evidence that every Ledger hardware device had been broken. Ledger’s security incident report.

The point is uncomfortable but necessary: a self-custody wallet can faithfully execute the wrong instruction. A convincing screen, urgent message, or apparently familiar website can induce that instruction.

Self-custody also leaves other risks intact. Asset prices can fall. Networks can become congested. Smart contracts can contain vulnerabilities. Some tokens give issuers administrative powers; holding their keys does not remove those powers. Hardware can fail, software can contain defects, and backups can be incomplete.

For someone unable to maintain safe recovery procedures, a well-chosen custody service may be preferable to an improvised setup they do not understand. The right response is to develop competence gradually. Moving everything at once out of fear can replace one serious risk with another.

The relevant question is which risks you can understand, reduce, and bear—not which product promises a life without risk.

A practical way to take control

Moving toward self-custody is a process of verification. It should feel deliberate.

  1. Separate trading from holding. Decide what actually needs to remain on an exchange for near-term activity. A convenient trading account does not have to become the permanent home of every asset you own.
  2. Create the wallet through a verified source. Use the provider’s authentic distribution channel. Never adopt a recovery phrase supplied by a stranger, a supposed support agent, or a website offering a pre-funded wallet.
  3. Understand the backup before adding meaningful funds. Know exactly what restores access, how it is protected, and what happens if your phone is lost. Check the wallet’s supported recovery procedure without entering secrets into a website, chat, or untrusted device. Never erase your only working wallet to “test” an uncertain backup.
  4. Check the asset and network on both ends. Similar names and matching-looking addresses are not enough. Confirm that the receiving wallet supports the exact asset on the exact withdrawal network, including any required memo or destination tag.
  5. Make a small test transfer. Verify receipt and the ability to use the funds before moving more. Where appropriate, test a small outgoing transaction too. A successful test establishes that particular route; it does not guarantee future safety.
  6. Keep long-term holdings away from casual signing. Consider hardware-backed arrangements for substantial holdings, and assess whether you can operate them safely. Use separate credentials for experimental activity. Read permissions and transaction details rather than approving by habit.
  7. Plan for loss, incapacity, and inheritance. A recovery method that only works while you are present and remember everything is unfinished. Document a secure process without leaving all the ingredients for theft together.

If an exchange has paused withdrawals, do not trust messages offering a special exit, priority approval, or paid recovery shortcut. Follow verified announcements and wait for the relevant withdrawal route to reopen. No legitimate support conversation requires your wallet’s recovery phrase.

These practices cannot guarantee safety. They can make control informed and usable.

Why we build Oath Wallet

Oath Wallet is built around a simple commitment: the wallet should serve the person who holds it. Our product overview describes that approach, and our source repository is available for inspection.

We believe a wallet should make receiving, holding, sending, and recovery understandable. A user should be able to distinguish a transaction from an approval, a backup from a login, and a wallet balance from a platform’s promise. Good design helps people notice the decisions that matter.

Our preference for self-custody does not give us permission to make absolute claims. Open source creates an opportunity for scrutiny; it is not proof that software has no vulnerabilities. A readable interface helps; it cannot remove the need for careful decisions. No wallet provider, including Oath Wallet, should ask people to abandon judgment in exchange for a reassuring brand.

The point is to place meaningful authority with the user and make the responsibilities of that authority clear.

The question to ask before the next incident

When an exchange suffers a breach, attention naturally turns to the amount stolen, the suspected attacker, and the size of the recovery fund. Those are essential facts. They are not the only facts a customer needs.

Ask a more personal question: if this institution closes its withdrawal system tonight, what can I still do with my assets tomorrow?

If the answer depends entirely on that institution’s timetable, you have identified a custody dependency. Strong authentication, visible reserves, and responsible incident management may reduce parts of the risk. They do not remove that dependency.

Bitget’s recovery efforts deserve fair reporting. Its breach still demonstrates why protection cannot be measured only by whether a company ultimately absorbs a loss. People also need the ability to act.

Self-custody, practiced carefully, gives that ability a different foundation: credentials you control, backups you understand, and transactions you choose to authorize.

A balance is reassuring. The authority to use it is what makes it yours in practice.

Reporting note: researched and updated on September 28, 2026. The Bitget investigation and withdrawal restoration remain in progress. Company statements are identified as such; attribution and preliminary technical explanations should not be treated as final forensic findings. The headline rounds the September 25 estimate of $387.5 million to $388 million, consistent with Bitget’s latest public account. This article is published by Oath Wallet, a self-custody wallet provider, and explains our editorial position rather than offering individualized investment advice.

Sources and further reading

  • Bitget: September 25 fund-tracing update and revised $387.5 million estimate.
  • Bitget: updated incident explanation, chronology, product distinction, and investigation status.
  • Bitget: phased withdrawal restoration schedule.
  • TRM Labs: Bitget investigation and fund-flow analysis. Its headline retains the earlier estimate.
  • The Block: Bitcoin withdrawals begin resuming, September 28, 2026.
  • PCAOB Office of the Investor Advocate: limitations of proof-of-reserve reports.
  • Mt. Gox trustee: July 2014 bankruptcy report and June 2024 repayment announcement.
  • U.S. Department of Justice: Bankman-Fried sentencing and customer-fund misuse.
  • FBI: attribution of the February 2025 Bybit theft.
  • Bybit: preliminary investigation update, February 26, 2025.
  • SEC investor bulletin: crypto asset custody basics.
  • Ledger: December 2023 Connect Kit security incident report.

items.title: Oath 3.5.5: A Better Feel for Every Transfer
items.summary: Meet Slide to Send, clearer transaction activity, better Max fee handling, and simpler transaction details. A complete guide with real app screenshots and a hands-on video.
items.content_html:
Sending a transaction has a few moments that deserve your full attention: the address, the amount, the fee, and the final decision to let it go. Everything around those moments should be easy to follow.

Oath 3.5.5 brings a new Slide to Send control, a clearer way to follow transactions, and more reliable fee handling when you use Max. It also tidies up the details you read afterward—and keeps ordinary screens where you left them when you return to the app.

This guide covers the changes across the 3.5.5 release, including the latest build, 59. The screenshots and video use Oath’s actual interface in iOS Simulator with demonstration balances, prices, addresses, and transaction results. No funds were signed or sent. The video’s confirmation timing is simulated; it is not a claim about network speed.

Slide to Send: the final decision stays under your thumb

The last action on Review Transfer is now a slider. Three animated arrows and a soft shimmer show the direction to move. The control follows the language of the interface: left to right in English, right to left in Arabic and other right-to-left languages.

There is a useful distinction between reaching the end and letting go. Oath sends only when you release after completing at least 90% of the slide. Keeping your finger down at the end does not send the transaction. You can still move back below the threshold and release to cancel the gesture.

As you slide, the existing blue capsule becomes more pronounced. Light, stepped haptic feedback helps you feel your progress, with a softer approach to the end. The return motion follows the distance you have moved, so a short attempt and an almost-complete slide do not snap back in the same way. On supported devices, these small details make the control feel like something you move, rather than a button you happen to drag.

Review Transfer with sample Dogecoin amounts and a demonstration recipient. The screen is a real Simulator capture; values are illustrative.

How to use it

  1. Choose the asset and recipient, then enter the amount you want to send.

  2. On Review Transfer, check the network, recipient, amount, and fee. If you changed transaction options, review those too.

  3. Place your finger on the circular handle and slide in the direction of the arrows.

  4. Change your mind? Move back below 90% before lifting your finger, or release an incomplete slide. Nothing is submitted by that gesture.

  5. Ready? Complete the slide and lift your finger. A short animated checkmark appears in the handle before the review sheet closes.

That first checkmark acknowledges your completed gesture. It is not blockchain confirmation. The transaction still has to be submitted and accepted by the network; its progress appears in the activity capsule.

Video: the real Oath slider, recorded in Simulator with demonstration data. An incomplete slide returns; a completed slide waits for release. Submission and confirmation are simulated. No real funds were sent.

When the fee is still loading

Before the transfer is ready, the slider explains what is happening with “Getting network fee…” and a native loading indicator in its handle. Once the fee is available and the transfer passes its checks, the control changes smoothly into its enabled state.

Returning to an unchanged transfer no longer unnecessarily starts the whole loading experience again. A usable fee presentation stays available while the app refreshes what it needs. Editing the transaction can still require new calculations, and network conditions can change. Always check the reviewed amount and fee before sending.

One place to follow a transaction

After submission begins, a capsule appears near the top of Home. The asset’s logo stays visible, with a small badge that changes as the transaction progresses. You no longer have to interpret the same “sent to network” message at every stage.

  • Sending… means Oath is working on submission. The badge is a loading indicator.

  • Transaction Sent means the submission was accepted. A dot marks this stage; it is not a confirmation checkmark.

  • Confirming… means the transaction is still waiting for the network’s confirmation. The badge shows a loading indicator.

  • Transaction Confirmed means the app has received confirmation evidence. The badge becomes a green checkmark.

  • Transaction Failed shows a danger badge. Open the transaction to read the specific result and any next step.

A connection problem or a temporarily unavailable result is not proof that a transaction failed. If the outcome is uncertain, Oath keeps that distinction rather than presenting an unverified success or failure.

A capsule that gets out of the way

Once you have seen a Confirming or Confirmed capsule, it dismisses itself after three seconds. That countdown continues if you move to another screen; you do not have to return to Home and watch it again. You can also swipe it upward to hide it yourself. Sent and Failed states remain available until dismissed rather than disappearing on the same automatic timer.

If a transaction confirms while its capsule is still visible, the existing capsule changes to Confirmed. If the capsule has already gone away, the confirmation can appear again as a new update for that same transaction, then dismiss after three seconds. A later failure can also bring the capsule back so the result is not missed.

Swiping away the capsule only hides the notification. It does not cancel a transaction that has already been submitted.

Several transfers? Open the bell

The bell beside the wallet selector appears when there is relevant transaction activity. Its number tells you how many items need attention. Tap it to open Activity, where you can follow pending incoming and outgoing transactions and relevant failures, then open an individual transaction for details.

The list keeps the information compact: the asset logo and status badge, the current status, the amount with its ticker, and a disclosure arrow. Repeated coin and network names have been removed from these rows. It uses the native navigation bar and close control, with the same glass presentation as the activity surface.

Activity opens from the bell and keeps each transfer compact. This is a simulated pending transaction in the real app interface.

The small capsule continues to show one transaction at a time. The bell is the place to check the wider picture, especially if you send more than one transfer before the earlier ones confirm.

Max now makes proper room for the fee

When you send a network’s native coin, the amount you can transfer must leave enough to pay that network’s costs. Choosing Max should account for that before you reach the final slide.

Version 3.5.5 improves this calculation, including a TRON issue where a Max transfer could fail with an insufficient-balance message even though the wallet had TRX. The available balance was being committed to the transfer before all applicable costs were properly reserved. Oath now makes room for the required costs before building the native TRX transfer.

For TRON, those costs can include bandwidth and, when applicable, recipient-account activation. Your resources, the recipient, and current network rules affect the result. A custom fee must also cover the required cost; setting it too low cannot make the network accept an underfunded transfer.

Illustrative TRON review: 98.9 TRX for the recipient and a 1.1 TRX fee from a 100 TRX demo balance. Actual fees vary.

Here is an illustrative example: if a wallet has 100 TRX and the required fee is 1.1 TRX, the transferable amount is 98.9 TRX. Those are demonstration numbers, not a fixed TRON fee. On networks that require an account reserve or a minimum remaining balance, that requirement must be retained too. Max means the maximum spendable amount, which is not always the entire displayed balance.

Native coins and tokens work differently

For a native-coin transfer, Max accounts for the fee in that same coin. For a token transfer, you can send the token balance, but the network fee still needs to be funded separately with the native coin on that network.

For example, sending a TRC-20 token requires enough TRX for its network fee. Holding a large token balance does not by itself cover that fee. Oath checks the native fee balance; it does not automatically sell tokens or subtract a token quantity as a substitute for native gas.

To use Max, choose the correct asset and network, enter the recipient, tap Max on the amount screen, and review the resulting amount and Network Fee before completing the slide. If a fee or reserve leaves no spendable amount, add the required funds or choose a smaller transfer when appropriate.

Bitcoin-family change: no more avoidable dust output

Bitcoin, Bitcoin Cash, Litecoin, and Dogecoin use unspent transaction outputs, or UTXOs. A transfer spends one or more outputs and usually returns the remainder to your wallet as change. That change is separate from the amount sent to the recipient.

Sometimes the leftover change is too small to create a valid, relayable output. This is called dust. A wallet can have enough total funds and still build a transaction the network rejects if it tries to create that tiny change output.

In 3.5.5, change below the applicable dust threshold is added to the network fee instead of being emitted as a dust UTXO. The calculation is handled consistently through review and transaction construction for the supported Bitcoin-family send paths.

This is particularly useful when spending several small outputs or sending almost everything. It removes an avoidable rejection without leaving a tiny output behind. The dust threshold depends on the network and output type, so there is no single dollar amount that applies everywhere.

The rule applies to the leftover change—not to the recipient’s payment. A recipient output that is itself below the network’s minimum still needs to be corrected. Always review the fee, including any small remainder absorbed into it. Coin Control remains available if you want to choose which UTXOs the transaction spends.

For more context on address types, derivation indexes, and Coin Control, see our complete Bitcoin settings guide.

Confirmation and balance updates that follow the transfer

A transaction can be confirmed on-chain while a wallet is still showing older information. This release improves the checks behind pending transactions across the app’s supported networks, including the Bitcoin Cash path that could leave a completed transfer looking pending.

After a send, Oath begins refreshing the affected network’s balance after approximately two seconds and follows up as the transaction’s result becomes available. Failed or rejected attempts also prompt a balance refresh. Pending transaction tracking can resume when you reopen the app.

That two-second point is the start of a balance check, not a promise that a blockchain or its data provider will have updated within two seconds. A balance that has not changed does not prove a send failed: the provider may be behind, and a transfer between your own addresses may produce a different balance change from a payment to someone else. Transaction status and balance evidence need to be considered together.

The practical improvement is less waiting for Oath to catch up after new information becomes available. It does not make blocks arrive faster, change a network’s finality rules, or allow unlimited polling while iOS has suspended the app.

Transaction details, with less repetition

The transaction screen has been simplified around the information you actually need to inspect. “Confirmation Pending” is now the shorter “Pending.” “Blockchain Network” becomes “Network,” and “Transfer Amount” becomes “Amount.” The network appears once in the overview rather than being repeated in the transfer summary.

The Transfer Summary now brings Amount and Network Fee together. The separate Value and Fee in US Dollar rows are gone. Both summary values start in your selected local currency; tap an available value to switch it to the relevant cryptocurrency unit, then tap again to switch back.

The simplified Transfer Summary brings Amount and Network Fee together. All transaction data shown here is demonstration data.

This keeps the summary short without taking away the precise coin amount. For a token transfer, remember that the amount and fee may be denominated in different assets: the token you sent and the native coin that paid the fee.

Tap Amount to switch the same value from local currency to cryptocurrency units. The fee has its own display toggle.

Interactive values now use the same neutral text treatment as the other fields. A disclosure arrow is reserved for a row that opens another screen or sheet. Tapping an amount to change its display does not need a navigation arrow because you stay on the same screen.

The transaction hash, sender, recipient, status, and local notes are still there when you need them. Notes remain on your iPhone and are not written into the blockchain transaction.

Come back to the screen you left

If you leave Oath while an ordinary transaction sheet is open, returning after a few minutes should not unexpectedly close it. Version 3.5.5 preserves that presentation while the app remains in memory, so you can continue reading where you stopped.

Screens that reveal sensitive wallet material are treated differently. A recovery phrase, private key, or other secret-reveal screen closes after about 20 seconds away. Your existing App Lock settings continue to apply; this change does not remove them.

As with other iOS apps, force-quitting the app or having iOS terminate it is different from switching away and returning. This improvement concerns resuming the running app, not a promise to restore every open sheet after a fresh launch.

A quieter Home and a tidier Receive screen

Home opens without the previous fade-and-scale entrance. The bottom settings control now uses a gear icon, making its purpose easier to recognize next to search.

Receive’s network filters have also been refined. The spacing beneath the title is tighter, and the chips fit their text and circular network artwork more naturally. Tap a network to narrow the asset list, or choose All to see the broader selection.

Receive uses content-sized network chips and tighter spacing beneath the navigation title. Assets and balances are samples.

Temporary refresh problems also receive better handling. Existing wallet content can remain visible instead of being interrupted by the technical wallet-refresh alert that exposed a timeout code. A temporary inability to refresh is not the same as losing your wallet or your funds.

Account-activation guidance is more selective too. On networks with a genuine activation or funding requirement, the amount screen surfaces the relevant shortfall when it matters. It avoids showing an unnecessary “not active” warning when the entered amount already satisfies the applicable requirement.

A few more fixes worth knowing about

  • Backup and private-key messages are clearer, with more specific wording for the material or action involved.

  • Import handles rejected phrase entries more cleanly when you choose to try a different phrase.

  • The send activity flow includes fixes for a background queue crash and for capsules that could linger after you had already seen them.

  • Slider movement, direction, and feedback have been refined for both left-to-right and right-to-left interfaces, including a smoother return while you move your finger back.

The common thread is straightforward: give you a clearer decision before a transfer, a clearer result afterward, and fewer interruptions in between.

Getting 3.5.5

Oath 3.5.5 is available on the App Store. Open the listing on your iPhone or iPad and choose Update if you already have Oath installed.

Once installed, the in-app Version History contains the notes for your exact version and build. Start with a transfer you can review carefully: check the recipient, inspect the fee, try moving the slider and returning it, and only complete and release it when you are ready to submit.

items.title: Inside Oath 3.5.4: Recovery With More Range
items.summary: A detailed guide to broader Bitcoin recovery, BRD wallets, Silent Payment output exports, clearer Coin Control, fee funding, and everyday improvements—with real app screenshots.
items.content_html:
An old Bitcoin backup is rarely just an old file. It is a record of decisions made by another wallet: how it derived addresses, where it put change, which script it used, and what it encrypted. Recovering the private key is only part of the job. The receiving wallet also has to understand what that key was meant to do.

Oath 3.5.4 puts much of its work into that less visible side of self-custody. It expands Bitcoin recovery, carries imported wallet collections through backup and migration, and adds a precise recovery route for individual Silent Payment outputs. Sending gets clearer coin selection and better checks that the wallet can actually pay the network fee. Notifications and everyday navigation receive attention, too.

This guide explains the changes across the 3.5.4 release, including build 55. The four screenshots are direct captures from build 55 in an iPhone simulator, using an empty demonstration wallet. They show the real interface; no recovery phrase or private key appears in them.

Availability note, September 13, 2026: this article covers 3.5.4 build 55. The public US App Store listing showed 3.5.3 when checked for publication. Check the App Store listing and your installed version before following a new workflow.

What deserves your attention

  • Recovering older Bitcoin wallets: more private-key formats, supported Bitcoin Core and Electrum files, and BRD address families.

  • Keeping a recovery complete: imported collections retain their keys, address policies, and derivation information through supported backup and transfer paths.

  • Recovering a Silent Payment output: export the full raw Taproot descriptor for an eligible unspent output, then import it without changing its meaning.

  • Choosing what to spend: Coin Control has its own place in Send, with address-type labels and a preview of automatic input selection.

  • Paying the network fee: Review checks native-coin funding, offers the relevant deposit address, and can reduce a native-coin send amount to leave room for fees.

  • Using the app day to day: clearer notifications, network and memo guidance, improved Solana loading and Sui transfers, and compatibility and layout fixes.

Bitcoin recovery starts with the right interpretation

Two wallets can hold the same private key and still display different addresses. Address construction matters. So do the derivation path and whether the original wallet was using a receiving branch or a change branch.

That is why importing a complete wallet file can be more useful than extracting a single key from it. A file may preserve information that a bare key does not: the script type, a saved account node, address ranges, or the point at which the old wallet should resume generating addresses.

In 3.5.4, Oath’s Bitcoin importer accepts a broader set of representations and keeps supported wallet structure with the keys. It validates the collection before creating the wallet. A damaged or unsupported entry should stop the import, rather than quietly leave you with a wallet containing only the first usable key.

A wider set of private-key formats

The Bitcoin private-key flow supports WIF, 32-byte HEX, BIP38 encrypted keys, checksummed mini private keys, and supported extended private keys such as xprv, yprv, and zprv. It also understands Electrum’s script-prefixed WIF representations and supported private output descriptors.

BIP38 is useful when an older backup contains an encrypted private key rather than a recovery phrase. Oath asks for its password using a secure native prompt. After successful decryption, the existing validation and import continue without requiring a second tap on Import. The password is the one protecting that encrypted key; it is not automatically your Oath app passcode or an optional BIP-39 passphrase. The format is defined in the BIP38 specification.

Descriptors carry instructions alongside key material. Supported policies include pkh for Legacy, wpkh for Native SegWit, sh(wpkh) for Nested SegWit, and supported key-path Taproot forms. Keeping an explicit policy prevents a valid key from being interpreted as an unrelated address type. Bitcoin Core’s descriptor documentation explains the distinction between the key and the script that uses it.

For a whole wallet, prefer its supported complete export over an isolated extended key. Pasting an extended key into a single-key entry is not a promise to recover every branch and address in the original wallet. File and ranged-descriptor imports have the additional structure needed to describe a collection.

Bitcoin Core files

Oath can read supported Bitcoin Core text exports and standalone wallet backups. These include legacy Berkeley DB v9 wallet.dat backups and SQLite descriptor-wallet backups, including the supported encrypted forms. Compatibility was verified during implementation with Bitcoin Core 28.3 outputs.

Use a complete backup produced by the original wallet. A database copied while it is in use may depend on separate journal files, and a file named wallet.dat is not automatically a complete or supported backup. Oath does not search arbitrary damaged binary data for anything that resembles a private key.

For structured exports, the importer also accepts TXT, supported CSV layouts, and supported JSON representations, including Bitcoin Core private-descriptor exports. A CSV needs a recognized key column; merely renaming an arbitrary file to .csv or .json does not convert it.

Electrum files

Support includes standard single-signature Electrum wallet files, imported-key wallets, old Electrum derivation, supported encrypted keystores, and BIE1 whole-file encryption. The importer preserves the saved node, script type, receive and change branches, and supported ranges and gap settings.

That last detail can make the difference between recovering the right wallet and deriving an entirely different set of addresses. A saved account node is already at a particular place in the tree. Its recorded origin must not be applied a second time.

There are deliberate limits. This importer does not restore Electrum multisignature or TrustedCoin two-factor workflows, watch-only or hardware-only wallets, BIE2 hardware-encrypted files, Lightning channels, or unsplit multi-account backups. It also rejects unsupported script policies, damaged files, and unrecognized future formats. General files are limited to 64 MiB; historical Python-literal Electrum files have a lower 16 MiB limit.

Across these file imports, unsupported policies include multisignature, P2WSH, miniscript, and Taproot script trees. A supported file container does not make every spending policy inside it supported.

These are Bitcoin mainnet recovery paths. They are not universal compatibility with every wallet that has ever stored Bitcoin keys. Keep the original backup and the software information needed to interpret it until you have checked the recovered wallet.

How to import a supported Bitcoin backup

In an existing Oath installation, start with the add-wallet control on Home.

  1. Choose Import an Existing Wallet.

  2. Select Private Key, then choose Bitcoin.

  3. For a supported key or descriptor, enter it, paste it, or scan its QR code. For a wallet file, tap Import a File and select the backup in Apple’s Files picker.

  4. Check the selected attachment. The file view shows its name and size when available; Replace chooses a different file and Clear removes the selection.

  5. Tap Import. If the backup is encrypted, provide its password in the secure prompt. A correct password continues the import automatically.

  6. Let the wallet discover its addresses and balances. Compare a known receiving address and the expected activity with the original wallet before treating recovery as complete.

Bitcoin import in Oath 3.5.4 (55). Import a File opens Apple’s Files picker. This demonstration contains no private key.

File parsing and password processing happen locally. Oath does not submit the backup or its password to a provider for conversion. After import, balance and transaction discovery still require network requests involving public wallet information. Local decryption should not be confused with an entirely offline wallet experience.

Importing does not move the coins. It gives another installation access to the same keys. The previous wallet can still control those funds. If a key was exposed before import, bringing it into Oath does not make that old key secret again.

BRD wallets get their own place in Bitcoin settings

The update adds BRD Legacy and BRD Native SegWit support across Bitcoin address derivation, discovery, balances, receiving, sending, change, and key export.

Older BRD wallets use a different account derivation convention from the familiar BIP44 or BIP84 account paths. Recovering the correct words while looking only at a different path can make an existing wallet appear empty. An empty balance in that situation does not establish that the coins are gone.

In Oath, the BRD families appear alongside the standard Bitcoin address types. For a recovery-phrase wallet, open Bitcoin, choose Receive, open the address-type menu, and choose Settings to inspect the available families. Your wallet’s imported material determines which policies are available; a single imported key does not necessarily support every family shown in a full recovery-phrase wallet.

A full recovery-phrase demonstration wallet in 3.5.4 (55). BRD Legacy and BRD Native SegWit appear beside the standard families. The generated-address count belongs to this empty example, not every wallet.

Choosing an address family for Receive changes which kind of address the app presents. It does not transfer your balance between formats. Existing coins remain at their existing outputs until a transaction spends them.

Address indexes still matter, especially for an older wallet that used custom ranges. Automatic discovery follows supported ranges and gap rules; it is not an unlimited search through every possible index. Our complete Bitcoin settings guide covers selecting indexes, generating address ranges, change, and the consequences of using unusually high indexes.

Back up the collection, not just one of its keys

A wallet recovered from a file may contain many independent keys or several derivation sources. A backup of one key can restore that key perfectly while missing the rest of the wallet.

Version 3.5.4 improves preservation of imported Bitcoin collections through Oath’s collection export, encrypted backup and restore, and direct device migration. The important material travels together: the secret collection and the supported address policies and derivation information needed to use it correctly.

After importing a collection, make a fresh complete backup through the appropriate Oath backup route. Keep the original source backup until you have verified recovery. Do not assume that recovery words from another wallet also cover independently imported keys.

If you are changing phones, update both installations before using the supported transfer workflow and verify the receiving device before erasing the old one. The direct iPhone transfer guide explains that process. Transfer is useful when both devices work; an independent backup is what you need when the old device is unavailable.

Silent Payment recovery: preserve the whole descriptor

Silent Payments already let a sender derive a fresh on-chain destination from a reusable payment address. The 3.5.4 change concerns recovery of an individual output you have received, rather than the introduction of Silent Payments themselves. The underlying protocol is described in BIP352.

An eligible unspent Silent Payment output can now be exported as a checksummed rawtr private descriptor. This is a precise instruction to use the supplied key as the final Taproot output key.

That wording matters. Ordinary Taproot construction can apply an additional key adjustment. If recovery software takes this output’s key and applies that adjustment again, it can derive a different destination. A private key can be mathematically valid and still be used with the wrong spending policy.

The rawtr descriptor preserves the intended meaning through supported text, QR, and file import, as well as backup and migration. Oath checks the output’s ownership before making it available for export. Spent or orphaned outputs are excluded from this recovery route.

How to use the output recovery route

  1. Open Bitcoin’s Receive screen and enter Settings from the address-type menu.

  2. Open Silent Payments and select an eligible unspent output.

  3. Choose Export Private Key and complete the app’s existing authorization when requested.

  4. Preserve the entire rawtr descriptor, including its checksum. Do not extract just the inner key or remove the surrounding policy.

  5. Import the complete descriptor into Oath or another wallet that explicitly supports this raw Taproot form, then verify that it resolves to the expected output.

The recovery screen contains spending material, so it is intentionally not pictured in this article. Treat both its QR code and text as a private key. Oath’s copy action is local to the device and expires after two minutes; that does not remove copies saved elsewhere.

This export covers the selected output. It does not replace the original wallet’s recovery material or provide a backup of future Silent Payments. Keep the recovery phrase, any applicable passphrase, and the information needed to restore and scan the original wallet. Our Silent Payments guide explains the wider receiving and scanning model.

Coin Control has a clearer job in Send

Bitcoin balances are made up of unspent transaction outputs, often called UTXOs. A transaction selects some of those outputs as inputs, pays the recipient, and normally returns any remainder as change. Choosing inputs affects the transaction’s size and can reveal relationships between previously separate outputs. The Bitcoin developer guide explains this input-and-output model.

In 3.5.4, Coin Control is separate from Network Fee in the amount screen’s options menu. This separates two decisions: which outputs to spend, and how to price the transaction’s fee.

Automatic selection now provides a preview of the inputs selected for the current amount and fee conditions. If you have not entered a positive amount, the app asks you to enter one before inspecting that selection. There is no meaningful payment to assemble yet.

Manual selection lets you choose specific available outputs. Address-type labels help identify what you are selecting, alongside amounts and confirmations. The selection belongs to the current send draft and is checked again as the transaction proceeds. Selecting too little to cover the payment and fee does not authorize the app to quietly add other inputs.

To inspect it, choose Bitcoin in Send, enter the recipient, continue to the amount screen, enter an amount, and open the options menu. Choose Coin Control to inspect automatic selection or make a manual choice. Use Network Fee when you want to change fee settings.

This release also corrects handling of manually selected inputs in the shared imported-wallet and Silent Payment signing path. The complete selected set is included when calculating fees, change, and signatures. A manual selection must mean the whole selection throughout the transaction.

Automatic selection is a sensible starting point when you do not need a particular set of outputs. Manual selection is useful when you have a reason to keep some outputs separate or spend specific ones. More inputs can mean a larger fee, and combining them can make their relationship visible on-chain. Coin Control provides a choice; it does not make a transaction anonymous.

Review now checks the coin that pays the fee

A token balance and a fee balance are different things. You can hold USDC on an EVM network and still lack the native coin needed to transfer it. On Ethereum, transaction gas is paid in ETH; see the official gas documentation. On other networks, use the fee asset required by that network.

For example, sending USDC on Arbitrum requires fee funding on Arbitrum. ETH sitting on Ethereum mainnet does not automatically fund that transaction. A large combined portfolio value cannot substitute for funds on the correct chain.

Version 3.5.4 strengthens the live funding check in Review. The flow checks the send amount and native fee requirement before allowing the transaction to proceed. When native fee funding is missing, it can open a deposit screen for the correct network’s native coin.

That deposit screen gives you the relevant receiving destination. It is not a swap, purchase, or bridge. Funds sent to it still need to arrive on the network shown.

Native-coin amounts can adjust to leave room for fees

When you send the network’s native coin, the payment and fee draw from the same balance. If the requested amount would leave too little for the estimated fee and any applicable reserve, Oath can reduce the send amount to what is available after those requirements.

This is not limited to tapping Max. It also applies when a manually entered native-coin amount exceeds what remains available after fees. If the requested amount already fits, it is preserved. If nothing usable remains, the flow cannot continue with a zero-value payment.

Read the amount in Review, especially when paying an exact invoice. If it has been reduced, the recipient would receive that smaller amount. Add sufficient funds or reconsider the payment before confirming. A later balance increase does not silently increase the already adjusted amount.

For token transfers, the token amount stays unchanged. You must fund the network fee separately in the required native coin. The app does not solve a missing gas balance by silently selling part of the token payment.

Notifications that are easier to act on

Notifications are most useful when you can understand them immediately and inspect what happened next. The update improves localized notification content, amount formatting, asset artwork, and the transaction details opened from an alert.

Open Settings → Notifications to review the master switch and the separate choices for incoming transfers, outgoing transfers, and announcements. The release improves how the notification experience follows those preferences.

Notification preferences in Oath 3.5.4 (55). These are the demonstration wallet’s current selections, not a recommendation or a statement of default settings.

Opening a transaction alert now leads to details that check the current transaction status. An earlier notification is a record of what was observed at that time, not a permanent guarantee of confirmation. If current details cannot be retrieved, the interface explains that limitation and offers a retry.

Amounts follow the notification’s localization and formatting context, with fiat information where available. Asset artwork helps distinguish the transaction being described. Delivery still depends on supported monitoring, network access, system notification permissions, and device delivery; this is not a promise that every event appears instantly.

The settings screen also explains the privacy boundary. The notification service receives public wallet addresses, device delivery information, and selected preferences. It does not receive recovery phrases or private keys for notification monitoring. Public addresses can still reveal financial activity, so this is a meaningful setting to review.

Smaller changes that matter in ordinary use

Receive names the network more precisely

Avalanche receiving now identifies Avalanche C-Chain. That is useful because “Avalanche” alone can be too vague when a sender or exchange offers several network choices. Match the actual destination network before sending.

Receive also explains the memo behavior for Oath-controlled Stellar and Gram addresses. A memo is not required for those wallet addresses. If the sending service requires one, the screen explains that a valid memo can be entered without changing receipt by your wallet.

Keep that guidance attached to its context. An exchange or another custodial recipient may require a particular memo to credit your deposit. The fact that your own Oath address does not need one says nothing about somebody else’s receiving requirements.

Solana loading and Sui transfers

Solana balance and history requests have been improved. For users, the purpose is straightforward: retrieve the information needed to understand the account more reliably.

Sui work addresses transfer submission, provider access failures, and transaction-history handling. An uncertain submission result is handled conservatively: the app attempts to reconcile what happened rather than automatically creating a new replacement transaction. A missing response does not necessarily mean nothing reached the network.

The release also fixes handling of fractional transaction timestamps on older iOS versions. These are reliability corrections, not a change to network confirmation rules or a guarantee against provider outages.

Layout, typing, and the details you edit

The update includes iOS 27 compatibility work, right-to-left layout corrections, clearer chain-specific recipient hints, keyboard stability fixes, and improved network-selector spacing. Translation corrections accompany these changes, and new release descriptions are available across the 57 shipped languages.

Transaction notes still save while you edit them. The extra checkmark has been removed from the Transaction Details navigation bar; the editing toolbar owns the save action, and Done also commits the note. The change removes duplicate controls without removing note editing.

Wikipedia asset descriptions have been removed. Asset identity, balances, and transaction actions remain the information to use when deciding what you are holding or sending.

Check your build, then try the changes that fit your wallet

Open Settings → About to see the installed version and build number. Version History now distinguishes builds within the same app version and provides expanded Bitcoin release descriptions.

The installed build is identified as 3.5.4 (55). Scroll within Version History to read the remaining notes and earlier builds.

If you already use Oath, installing an update does not mean you should erase your wallet or repeat an import. Start with the changes relevant to you: inspect Coin Control before your next Bitcoin send, read the amount and fee funding in Review, and check your notification preferences.

If you are recovering an older wallet, take more time. Identify the original format, choose a supported complete backup, compare known addresses, and verify the result before retiring the original recovery route. If the wallet contains imported keys, make sure your new backup covers the entire collection.

The value of 3.5.4 is in these concrete moments: an older backup retaining its meaning, a Silent Payment output recovering to the correct destination, a manual input selection staying intact, and a fee requirement appearing before you authorize the payment.

Self-custody gives you the final decision. The wallet should give you enough accurate information to make it.

items.title: Bitcoin Address Types and Recovery Scope in Oath
items.summary: Match the address type and imported key scope; changing the visible format does not change the blockchain.
items.content_html:
Updated October 30, 2026 · source 4.1.14 (98)

Current release guidance

Checked against the 4.1.14 source. No Apple upload has been started for build 98; check the version installed on your phone. Older screenshots are illustrative and may show controls absent from this release.

Available address families

For compatible Bitcoin wallets, Receive offers Taproot (BIP86), Native SegWit (BIP84), nested SegWit (BIP49) and Legacy (BIP44). The available choices depend on your imported material. An uncompressed single key supports Legacy only; a scoped extended key cannot recreate unrelated branches.

Receive and change

A new receiving address can belong to the same wallet. Change addresses account for value returned to your wallet by a transaction. The scan covers supported imported branches rather than only the currently selected display type. It does not guarantee discovery beyond the implemented account and gap rules.

Electrum and aezeed

These are Bitcoin-specific recovery formats. Preserve the original seed extension or password. Aezeed account-zero recovery covers supported on-chain paths; it does not recover Lightning channels or arbitrary custom accounts.

Unsupported recovery methods

Silent Payments receiving and discovery are not supported in 4.1.14. Do not treat an sp1 destination as ordinary Taproot, and do not assume an old BRD-specific recovery menu or screenshot exists in this build. Keep the original wallet when the required account format is unsupported.

Before sending or receiving

Confirm the exact network, full recipient address and required fee. Refresh and compare known addresses before relying on a restore. A published example address or screenshot is not a receiving address for your wallet.

See the current security model, Help Center, and release verification record. Never share recovery words, private keys or backup passwords with support.

items.title: WalletConnect in Oath: Review the Request, Control the Permission
items.summary: Oath now supports WalletConnect. Understand the difference between a session, a signature and an on-chain approval.
items.content_html:
Updated October 30, 2026 · source 4.1.14 (98)

Current release guidance

Checked against the 4.1.14 source. No Apple upload has been started for build 98; check the version installed on your phone. Older screenshots are illustrative and may show controls absent from this release.

What changed

Earlier Oath versions did not include WalletConnect. That older product boundary no longer describes 4.1.14: supported dApps can connect through encrypted WalletConnect relay sessions. Use the current connection screens and supported-chain guidance.

Connection is not unlimited approval

Review the dApp identity, proposed accounts and networks before connecting. Public account access does not justify every later transaction or signature. Read each request and decline anything you cannot explain.

Transactions and swaps

A dApp can prepare a swap or another contract interaction. The wallet reviews and signs supported requests locally after approval. The route, contracts, recipient and spending authority still matter; a readable screen or familiar dApp name is not a guarantee of safety.

Disconnect versus revoke

Disconnecting closes a session. Existing on-chain token or account permissions can remain until a supported revocation transaction succeeds. Revocations require fees and can fail; multiple revocations are not one atomic operation.

Keep recovery material private

A legitimate connection uses public accounts and requested signatures, not your recovery phrase or private key. Never type recovery material into a dApp, support message or web-based troubleshooting form.

See the current security model, Help Center, and release verification record. Never share recovery words, private keys or backup passwords with support.

items.title: Coldcard’s Weak-Seed Crisis: Complexity Is Not the Same as Security
items.summary: The 2026 Coldcard incident did not remotely compromise the devices. It exposed something more fundamental: a sophisticated enclosure cannot protect a seed that was predictable at birth.
items.content_html:
Research note, September 3, 2026. This article distinguishes confirmed facts, vendor statements, on-chain estimates, and our own analysis. Coinkite’s formal technical postmortem was still unpublished when this article was prepared. Loss totals changed as investigators attributed additional transactions, so figures below are dated snapshots rather than a final accounting.

In July 2026, Bitcoin disappeared from thousands of addresses whose owners believed their keys were protected by Coldcard hardware wallets. The first and most important correction is also the most revealing: the devices were not remotely taken over. A firmware error had weakened the randomness used when some wallets were created. Attackers could search the reduced key space elsewhere, recover candidate private keys, compare derived addresses with the public Bitcoin blockchain, and spend matching funds without touching the hardware.

A vault can be physically formidable and still fail if the secret placed inside it was predictable from the beginning.

That is why this incident matters far beyond one vendor. It challenges a comforting shortcut: hardware equals secure, more components equal more protection, and a long feature list equals high assurance. None of those statements is a threat model. Security comes from the complete system—entropy, firmware, hardware, build process, distribution, interface, backups, operator behavior, and physical safety—and from evidence that lets outsiders test its claims.

What happened to Coldcard

Coinkite’s official advisory says affected firmware used a faulty seed-generation path. Wallet seeds created on Mk2 or Mk3 firmware 4.0.1 through 4.1.9 were at risk unless sufficient private, independent dice entropy had been added or a strong, unique BIP39 passphrase created an additional barrier. The advisory also covers seeds generated on Mk4, Mk5, and Q devices before their fixed standard or Edge releases.
